### Problem: Partition Array According to Given Pivot {#sec-part-p1-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `nums` of $n$ integers ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^6 \le \text{nums}[i] \le 10^6$) and a value `pivot` that occurs in `nums`. Rearrange `nums` so that:

1. every element **strictly less than** `pivot` appears before every element **equal to** it,
2. every element **equal to** `pivot` appears before every element **strictly greater than** it, and
3. the **relative order inside the "less" group and inside the "greater" group is preserved** (the rearrangement is *stable*).

Return the rearranged array. An output that satisfies (1) and (2) but breaks (3) is wrong.

Source: [LC 2161 · Partition Array According to Given Pivot](https://leetcode.com/problems/partition-array-according-to-given-pivot/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `nums = [9,12,3,5,14,10,7,6,21]`, `pivot = 10` → `[9,3,5,7,6,10,12,14,21]`. The values below 10 appear as `9,3,5,7,6`, the same order as in the input, and the values above 10 as `12,14,21`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A stable three-way partition: classify every element as less, equal or greater, and write each group in input order. Appending (never swapping) is what keeps the order, so the price of clause (3) is an output buffer; with one buffer, "less" fills from the front, "greater" fills from the back while scanning backwards, and the pivot copies fill the gap.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Three passes.** Read the definition literally: one pass copies every `x < pivot`, a second every `x == pivot`, a third every `x > pivot`. $O(n)$ time with three reads of the input, $O(n)$ output. Stable because every pass reads left to right.
2. **One scan, three lists.** Classify each element once and append it to `less`, `equal` or `greater`; concatenate at the end. Same bounds, one read of the input.
3. **One buffer, two write cursors.** Skip the three lists. Walk `i` from the left and, in the same loop, `n-1-i` from the right: a small value read from the left goes to `res[lo++]`, a large value read from the right goes to `res[hi--]`. Whatever is left between `lo` and `hi` is the pivot. Scanning the right end backwards and writing backwards keeps the "greater" group in input order.

**Invariant (form 2).** After reading `nums[0..k)`, `less` is the subsequence of `nums[0..k)` below the pivot, in input order, and the same holds for `equal` and `greater`.

**Invariant (form 3).** After step $i$, `res[0..lo)` is the subsequence of `nums[0..i]` below the pivot in input order, and `res(hi..n)` is the subsequence of `nums[n-1-i..n)` above the pivot in input order. After the loop both scans have read the whole array, so the gap `res[lo..hi]` has exactly as many cells as there are copies of the pivot.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Three passes

::: {.form-next}
Walk the array three times, once per group; each pass appends only its own elements. $O(n)$ time with three reads, $O(n)$ output. This is the oracle the later forms are tested against.

**Worked example.** $[9,12,3,5,14,10,7,6,21]$ with pivot $10$: pass 1 copies $9,3,5,7,6$; pass 2 copies $10$; pass 3 copies $12,14,21$.
:::

```{python}

def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("pivot", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "[9, 3, 5, 7, 6, 10, 12, 14, 21]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def pivot_brute(nums, p):
    res = []
    for x in nums:
        if x < p:
            res.append(x)
    for x in nums:
        if x == p:
            res.append(x)
    for x in nums:
        if x > p:
            res.append(x)
    return res
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
vector<int> pivotBrute(const vector<int>& nums, int p) {
    vector<int> res;
    res.reserve(nums.size());
    for (int x : nums) if (x < p) res.push_back(x);
    for (int x : nums) if (x == p) res.push_back(x);
    for (int x : nums) if (x > p) res.push_back(x);
    return res;
}
```
:::

#### One scan, three lists

::: {.form-next}
Fuse the three passes. One cursor reads the input once; each element is compared with the pivot once and appended to its group. Same $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space, but the input is read once, which matters when it is a stream or when classifying is expensive.

**Worked example.** After $9$: less $=[9]$. After $12$: greater $=[12]$. After $3, 5$: less $=[9,3,5]$. After $14$: greater $=[12,14]$. After $10$: equal $=[10]$. After $7, 6$: less $=[9,3,5,7,6]$. After $21$: greater $=[12,14,21]$. Concatenate.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "[9, 3, 5, 7, 6, 10, 12, 14, 21]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-2161-threelist
def pivot_three_lists(nums, p):
    less, equal, greater = [], [], []
    for x in nums:
        if x < p:
            less.append(x)
        elif x == p:
            equal.append(x)
        else:
            greater.append(x)
    return less + equal + greater


for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(-20, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 15))]
    pv = random.choice(nums)
    assert pivot_three_lists(nums, pv) == pivot_brute(nums, pv)
print("pivot_three_lists OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
vector<int> pivotThreeLists(const vector<int>& nums, int p) {
    vector<int> less_, equal_, greater_;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x < p) less_.push_back(x);
        else if (x == p) equal_.push_back(x);
        else greater_.push_back(x);
    }
    vector<int> res(less_);
    res.insert(res.end(), equal_.begin(), equal_.end());
    res.insert(res.end(), greater_.begin(), greater_.end());
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> v{9, 12, 3, 5, 14, 10, 7, 6, 21};
    return pivotThreeLists(v, 10)[5] == 10 ? 0 : 1;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The three lists are the whole state. Each list only ever grows at its tail, so it is the subsequence of `nums` in its group, in input order: the invariant, written as code.

#### One buffer, two write cursors

::: {.form-next}
Drop the three lists and write straight into one result array. In step $i$, the front scan reads `nums[i]` and writes it at `res[lo]` if it is small; the back scan reads `nums[n-1-i]` and writes it at `res[hi]` if it is large. After $n$ steps the cells between the two cursors are exactly the pivot's copies. Still $O(n)$ time; the extra memory is the output alone, which is what the problem asks you to return.

**Worked example.** Step $0$ reads $9$ (small, `res[0] = 9`) and $21$ (large, `res[8] = 21`); step $2$ reads $3$ and $7$ (only $3$ is written; $7$ is small, and the front scan will meet it at step $6$); after step $8$, `lo = 5` and `hi = 5`, so `res[5] = 10`.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("pivot", "twoend")
    assert str(final) == "[9, 3, 5, 7, 6, 10, 12, 14, 21]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-2161-twoend
def pivot_array(nums, p):
    n = len(nums)
    res = [p] * n                        # the gap left at the end already holds p
    lo, hi = 0, n - 1
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] < p:                  # front scan: small values, in order
            res[lo] = nums[i]
            lo += 1
        if nums[n - 1 - i] > p:          # back scan: large values, written backwards
            res[hi] = nums[n - 1 - i]
            hi -= 1
    return res


for _ in range(2000):
    nums = [random.randint(-6, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 14))]
    pv = random.choice(nums)
    assert pivot_array(nums, pv) == pivot_brute(nums, pv)
assert pivot_array([9, 12, 3, 5, 14, 10, 7, 6, 21], 10) == [9, 3, 5, 7, 6, 10, 12, 14, 21]   # the board sample
assert pivot_array([-3, 4, 3, 2], 2) == [-3, 2, 4, 3]       # official sample 2
assert pivot_array([5], 5) == [5] and pivot_array([2, 2, 2], 2) == [2, 2, 2]
print("pivot_array OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
vector<int> pivotArray(const vector<int>& nums, int p) {
    int n = (int)nums.size(), lo = 0, hi = n - 1;
    vector<int> res(n, p);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (nums[i] < p) res[lo++] = nums[i];
        if (nums[n - 1 - i] > p) res[hi--] = nums[n - 1 - i];
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> v{9, 12, 3, 5, 14, 10, 7, 6, 21};
    vector<int> r = pivotArray(v, 10);
    return (r[0] == 9 && r[5] == 10 && r[8] == 21) ? 0 : 1;
}
```
:::
:::

**Why the in-place three-way partition is wrong here.** The Dutch national flag walk (@sec-part-dnf) produces `[< p | == p | > p]` in place with $O(1)$ extra memory, but it swaps elements across the array, and a swap can carry a value past others of its own group. On the sample it returns the right *groups* in the wrong *order*:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("pivot", "dnf")
    assert str(final) == "[9, 6, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 12]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

```{python}
#| label: arr-2161-dnf
def pivot_dnf(nums, p):
    """In-place three-way partition (Dutch national flag): right groups, unstable."""
    a = list(nums)
    lo, mid, hi = 0, 0, len(a) - 1
    while mid <= hi:
        if a[mid] < p:
            a[lo], a[mid] = a[mid], a[lo]
            lo += 1
            mid += 1
        elif a[mid] == p:
            mid += 1
        else:
            a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]
            hi -= 1
    return a


sample = [9, 12, 3, 5, 14, 10, 7, 6, 21]
res = pivot_dnf(sample, 10)
assert sorted(res) == sorted(sample)
assert res == [x for x in res if x < 10] + [x for x in res if x == 10] + [x for x in res if x > 10]
assert res == [9, 6, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 12] != pivot_array(sample, 10)   # groups right, order wrong
print("pivot_dnf: correct groups, unstable order")
```

Look at the "greater" group: the input has $12, 14, 21$, the walk returns $14, 21, 12$, because the first `swap(mid, hi)` sent $12$ to the far end. Stability needs the buffer; the in-place walk is the right tool only when the order inside a group does not matter, as in Sort Colors (@sec-pf-p1-colors).

::: {.p-complexity}
**Three passes**: $O(n)$ time (three reads), $O(n)$ output. **One scan, three lists**: $O(n)$ time (one read), $O(n)$ extra for the lists plus the output. **One buffer, two write cursors**: $O(n)$ time, no memory beyond the returned array. The in-place walk would be $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra, but it breaks clause (3).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **The pivot is the minimum or the maximum**: one outer group is empty; `lo` stays $0$ or `hi` stays $n-1$, and the gap still has the right size.
- **All elements equal the pivot**: nothing is written; the initial `res = [p] * n` is the answer.
- **$n = 1$**: the single element is the pivot (it must occur in `nums`).
- **Duplicates inside a group**: this is where stability is visible; both scans keep input order because each writes in the direction it reads.
- **Pivot missing** (not allowed by the statement): forms 1 and 2 still work; form 3 would leave a gap filled with a value that is not in the input, so check the precondition if you reuse the code.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1851B · Parity Sort](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1851/B){rating="800"} — swaps are allowed only inside a parity class, so each class keeps its slots: classify, sort each class, and compare with the sorted array.
- [LC 75 · Sort Colors](https://leetcode.com/problems/sort-colors/){difficulty="Medium"} — the same three groups when order inside a group does not matter, so the in-place walk is accepted (@sec-pf-p1-colors).
- [LC 905 · Sort Array By Parity](https://leetcode.com/problems/sort-array-by-parity/){difficulty="Easy"} — two groups, any order: the in-place version of this problem.
:::
